deep.reconstruction:
The page is one sheet of a large hand-drawn table of quadratic residue characters. It continues from fol. 9r, which has columns 227–359, and runs on to fol. 10, which has columns 509–659. On this sheet the columns are the primes 367, 373, …, 503, written at the top and bottom. The rows are the primes 439, 443, …, 503, 509, 521, and in red 523.

The rule for an entry, which I verified on many cells (my verification, not stated on the page), is this. A small circle stands in cell (row p, column q) exactly when q is a quadratic residue mod p, i.e. Legendre symbol (q/p) = +1.

The direction matters when p ≡ q ≡ 3 (mod 4), because then (q/p) = −(p/q). Example: (367/523) = +1 but (523/367) = −1, and the circle is present at (523, 367). So the circle means 'column prime is a residue of the row prime'.

The diagonal cells (p, p) also carry circles, e.g. (439,439), (443,443) and (449,449). Gauss apparently counts 0 among the residues.

Worked checks:
- Row 523 (red). Circles at 367, 383, 397, 419, 439, 443, 461, 467, 491, 503. These are exactly the column primes q with (q/523) = 1.
  - (367/523) = −(523/367) = −(156/367) = −(3/367)(13/367) = −(−1)(1) = +1.
  - (373/523) = (150/373) = (2/373)(3/373) = −1, so no circle.
  - (409/523) = (114/409) = (2/409)(3/409)(19/409) = 1·1·(10/19) = −1, so no circle.
  - (419/523) = −(104/419) = −(2/419)(13/419) = +1, so a circle.
- Row 439. Circles at 373, 379, 397, 409, 433, (439), 443, 449, 457, 461, 467, 479, 491, 503. These match (q/439) = 1.
  - (443/439) = (4/439) = 1.
  - (457/439) = (18/439) = (2/439) = 1, since 439 ≡ 7 (mod 8).
  - (463/439) = (24/439) = (3/439) = −1, so no circle.
  - (503/439) = (64/439) = 1.
- Row 443. (367/443) = +1 and (457/443) = (14/443) = +1, both circled. (449/443) = (6/443) = −1, not circled.
- Row 503. The chain 367–397 is all residues, e.g. (373/503) = (130/373) = (−1)(−1)(1) = +1.

Rows 509 and 521 are still empty in black ink; row 523 was added in red. The previous page also has a red row 541.

In addition, every pair of horizontally or vertically adjacent circles is joined by a line. This produces 'chains' and closed 'squares' — the clusters of neighbouring residues. There is no computation on the page beyond the table itself.

The purpose is evidently empirical tabulation of the residue character of primes against primes. This is the kind of material Gauss used for induction on quadratic reciprocity and for residue tables. It is analogous to Tabula II of the Disquisitiones (1801), but much larger: rows up to 541, columns up to 659. Why the adjacent residues are joined is not explained. It may be a visual device for checking or for spotting patterns (my conjecture).
errors: No errors found in the cells checked (rows 439, 443, 503, 523 and several individual cells): circles coincide with legendre_symbol(q,p)=1.
Diagonal cells (p,p) are marked with circles; this is a convention (0 counted with the residues), not an error.
Rows 509 and 521 are left blank, i.e. the table is incomplete on this sheet.

results.what: Table of quadratic residue characters (q/p) for column primes 367–503 against row primes 439–523, with circle = q is a quadratic residue mod p
results.modern_name: Table of Legendre symbols / quadratic residue table for primes
results.usually_credited_to: Residue tables: Euler, Legendre, Gauss (Disquisitiones Arithmeticae 1801, Tabula II); later large tables by Jacobi (Canon Arithmeticus 1839) and others

results.what: Graphical linking of horizontally/vertically adjacent residue entries into chains and squares
results.modern_name: Visualization of the quadratic residue pattern (no standard name)

deep.surprise_reason: Gauss's extensive empirical residue tables, and their role in his discovery and proof of quadratic reciprocity, are well documented. This sheet is a routine, accurate portion of such a table. The connecting-line visualization is a curiosity, not a mathematical result.
